title: Εὐρύπυλος βεβλημένος
source: Homer, The Iliad, Greek text of D. B. Monro and T. W. Allen, Homeri Opera, tomi I–II, 3rd ed. (Oxford Classical Texts; Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1920), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-greekLit tlg0012.tlg001.perseus-grc2, sha256 ae8b617018c6e5af. Text as printed: the edition sets no quotation marks round speeches, and none are added. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca — an admitted convention; Homer's own pronunciation was older and is not recoverable in detail. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; ï for a separately sounded ι; accents omitted). Scansion: made by program from the text and checked; it shows one defensible reading of each line, and the notes say where a line is irregular. All translations were made fresh from the Greek for Lectorium.
about: Nestor’s speech has stirred Patroclus, and he runs along the ships towards Achilles. At the ships of Odysseus, where the Achaeans hold their assembly and have their altars, he meets Eurypylus limping from the fighting with an arrow in his thigh, bleeding but clear in his mind. Patroclus pities him and asks whether the Achaeans can still hold Hector. Eurypylus answers that there is no longer any defence: the best men lie wounded and the Trojans grow stronger. He begs to be taken to a ship and treated, with the arrow cut out and the wound washed and dressed with the drugs Achilles taught Patroclus, since both healers, Podalirius and Machaon, are out of reach. Patroclus says he is on his way with Nestor’s message to Achilles, but will not abandon Eurypylus. He takes him to his hut, has hides spread, cuts out the arrow, washes the wound and lays on a bitter root that kills the pain; the wound dries and the blood stops.

sentences.t:
ὣς φάτο, τῷ δ’ ἄρα θυμὸν ἐνὶ στήθεσσιν ὄρινε,
βῆ δὲ θέειν παρὰ νῆας ἐπ’ Αἰακίδην Ἀχιλῆα.
sentences.tr:
hōs phato, tōi d’ ara thymon eni stēthessin orine,
bē de theein para nēas ep’ Aiakidēn Achilēa.
sentences.l:
So he spoke, and in him the heart in his breast he stirred,
and went to run along the ships to the descendant of Aeacus, Achilles.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and he stirred the heart in Patroclus’ breast, and Patroclus set off running along the ships to Achilles, descendant of Aeacus.
sentences.n: ὣς φάτο, τῷ δ’ ἄρα θυμὸν ἐνὶ στήθεσσιν ὄρινε is a formula of effect, ‘so he spoke, and he stirred the heart in his breast’; the speaker is Nestor, whose long speech ended in the last part, and τῷ ‘in him’ is Patroclus. The English is the one this line already has, with the name changed. Here the line ends in a comma, because the sentence runs on into βῆ δὲ θέειν. ὄρινε is an unaugmented aorist of ὀρίνω ‘stir up’, βῆ an unaugmented aorist of βαίνω ‘go’ (Attic ἔβη), and θέειν the uncontracted infinitive of θέω ‘run’ (Attic θεῖν): ‘went to run’, ‘set off running’. Αἰακίδην is a patronymic used for Achilles, ‘descendant of Aeacus’; Ἀχιλῆα has single λ.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὅτε δὴ κατὰ νῆας Ὀδυσσῆος θείοιο
ἷξε θέων Πάτροκλος, ἵνά σφ’ ἀγορή τε θέμις τε
ἤην, τῇ δὴ καί σφι θεῶν ἐτετεύχατο βωμοί,
sentences.tr:
all’ hote dē kata nēas Odyssēos theioio
hixe theōn Patroklos, hina sph’ agorē te themis te
ēēn, tēi dē kai sphi theōn eteteuchato bōmoi,
sentences.l:
But when now along the ships of divine Odysseus
he came running, Patroclus, where for them assembly and custom
was, there where indeed for them the altars of the gods had been built,
sentences.i: But when Patroclus came running along the ships of divine Odysseus to where they had their assembly and their settled custom, where the altars of the gods had been built for them,
sentences.n: This is a clause of time that waits for its main clause: the sentence is finished by ἔνθά οἱ … ἀντεβόλησε in the next unit. ἷξε is the aorist of ἵκω ‘come, reach’, unaugmented, with θέων ‘running’. Ὀδυσσῆος θείοιο is ‘of divine Odysseus’; θεῖος ‘divine’ is kept apart from δῖος ‘heavenly’. ἵνά σφ’ is ἵνα σφι ‘where for them’, σφι the dative plural of the pronoun. ἀγορή is the ‘assembly’; θέμις is what is settled as right by custom, and the two together name the place where the army met and judged. ἤην is a Homeric form of the imperfect of εἰμί (Attic ἦν; ἦεν is another Homeric form, as at 813), here singular for the pair of nouns. ἐτετεύχατο is the pluperfect passive of τεύχω ‘make, build’ with the epic ending -ατο (= Attic -ντο): ‘had been built’.

sentences.t:
ἔνθά οἱ Εὐρύπυλος βεβλημένος ἀντεβόλησε
διογενὴς Εὐαιμονίδης κατὰ μηρὸν ὀϊστῷ
σκάζων ἐκ πολέμου·
sentences.tr:
entha hoi Eurypylos beblēmenos antebolēse
diogenēs Euaimonidēs kata mēron oïstōi
skazōn ek polemou·
sentences.i: there Eurypylus, Zeus-born son of Euaemon, wounded in the thigh by an arrow, met him, limping from the war;
sentences.n: ἔνθά οἱ ‘there to him’ is the main clause the last unit was waiting for; οἱ is the dative of the pronoun (Attic αὐτῷ), meaning Patroclus, the one who is met: ἀντεβόλησε ‘met, came face to face’ takes the dative. βεβλημένος is the perfect passive participle of βάλλω ‘strike’, ‘struck’ in the literal line, ‘wounded’ in the free line. διογενής ‘Zeus-sprung’ (‘Zeus-born’) is a stock epithet, translated every time. Εὐαιμονίδης is a patronymic, ‘son of Euaemon’. κατὰ μηρόν ‘in the thigh’ goes with βεβλημένος, and ὀϊστῷ (the edition prints the diaeresis) is the dative of means, ‘with an arrow’. σκάζων is the present participle of σκάζω ‘limp’.

sentences.t:
κατὰ δὲ νότιος ῥέεν ἱδρὼς
ὤμων καὶ κεφαλῆς, ἀπὸ δ’ ἕλκεος ἀργαλέοιο
αἷμα μέλαν κελάρυζε·
sentences.tr:
kata de notios rheen hidrōs
ōmōn kai kephalēs, apo d’ helkeos argaleoio
haima melan kelaryze·
sentences.i: and wet sweat ran down from his shoulders and his head, and from the grievous wound dark blood came gurgling out;
sentences.n: Two verbs are split from their prefixes (tmesis): κατὰ … ῥέεν ‘ran down’ and ἀπὸ … κελάρυζε ‘gurgled from’. ῥέεν is the uncontracted, unaugmented imperfect of ῥέω (Attic ἔρρει). νότιος means ‘moist, wet’ and goes with ἱδρώς ‘sweat’. ὤμων καὶ κεφαλῆς are genitives of the place the sweat runs from, ‘from his shoulders and head’; ἕλκεος is the epic genitive of ἕλκος (Attic ἕλκους) and ἀργαλέοιο the genitive in -οιο, ‘grievous’. αἷμα μέλαν is ‘dark blood’, the house rendering of the colour word. κελαρύζω is ‘flow with a gurgling sound’.

sentences.t: νόος γε μὲν ἔμπεδος ἦεν.
sentences.tr: noos ge men empedos ēen.
sentences.l: but his mind at least was firm.
sentences.i: but his mind, at least, was firm.
sentences.n: γε μέν ‘but, yet, at least’ sets the one sound thing against the wounds just described: his body is hurt, but his νόος ‘mind’ is ἔμπεδος ‘firm’. νόος is the uncontracted form (Attic νοῦς). ἦεν is the epic imperfect of εἰμί, ‘was’, the same verb as ἤην in 808 in another form. It is why Eurypylus can speak so clearly and give instructions.

sentences.t:
τὸν δὲ ἰδὼν ᾤκτειρε Μενοιτίου ἄλκιμος υἱός,
καί ῥ’ ὀλοφυρόμενος ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα·
sentences.tr:
ton de idōn ōikteire Menoitiou alkimos huios,
kai rh’ olophyromenos epea pteroenta prosēuda·
sentences.l:
And him seeing, pitied Menoetius’ sturdy son,
and so, lamenting, winged words he spoke:
sentences.i: Menoetius’ sturdy son pitied him when he saw him, and, lamenting, he spoke winged words:
sentences.n: τὸν δὲ ἰδών ‘and seeing him’: τόν is the pronoun, Eurypylus. ᾤκτειρε is the aorist of οἰκτίρω ‘pity’, with augment. Μενοιτίου ἄλκιμος υἱός is the stock naming of Patroclus, ‘Menoetius’ sturdy son’, translated every time; ἄλκιμος ‘sturdy’ is built on ἀλκή ‘might’. καί ῥ’ is καὶ ῥα ‘and so’, ὀλοφυρόμενος ‘lamenting’, and ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα ‘winged words he spoke’ is the formula that introduces a speech; its English is the one it has where it stands in an earlier part. The speech follows.

sentences.t:
ἆ δειλοὶ Δαναῶν ἡγήτορες ἠδὲ μέδοντες
ὣς ἄρ’ ἐμέλλετε τῆλε φίλων καὶ πατρίδος αἴης
ἄσειν ἐν Τροίῃ ταχέας κύνας ἀργέτι δημῷ.
sentences.tr:
a deiloi Danaōn hēgētores ēde medontes
hōs ar’ emellete tēle philōn kai patridos aiēs
asein en Troiēi tacheas kynas argeti dēmōi.
sentences.l:
“Oh, miserable ones, leaders and lords of the Danaans,
so then you were destined, far from your dear ones and from your fatherland,
to glut in Troy the swift dogs with white fat.
sentences.i: “Oh, you miserable leaders and lords of the Danaans, so it was to be, then, that far from your dear ones and your fatherland you would glut the swift dogs in Troy with your white fat.
sentences.n: Patroclus’ cry is a lament, and ἆ ‘oh’ is its first sound. δειλοί here is ‘miserable’ in the sense of pitiable, not ‘cowardly’. Δαναῶν ἡγήτορες ἠδὲ μέδοντες is the standing phrase for the chiefs, ‘leaders and lords of the Danaans’. ὣς ἄρ’ ἐμέλλετε is the imperfect of μέλλω with an infinitive: ‘so, it seems, you were bound (destined) to…’. τῆλε φίλων καὶ πατρίδος αἴης is ‘far from your dear ones and fatherland’, with τῆλε taking the genitive; αἴης is the Ionic form of αἶα ‘land’. ἄσειν is an infinitive of ἄω ‘sate, glut’, with the dogs as object and the fat (δημῷ, dative of means) as what they are glutted with. The Greek does not say whose fat, but it is the chiefs’ own. ἀργέτι is an epic form meaning ‘white’.

sentences.l:
But come, tell me this, Zeus-nurtured one, Eurypylus, hero:
whether still, I wonder, the Achaeans will hold back huge Hector,
or already they will perish, by him with the spear subdued?”
sentences.i: But come now, tell me this, Zeus-nurtured one, Eurypylus, hero: will the Achaeans, I wonder, still hold huge Hector back, or will they already perish at his hands, overcome by the spear?”
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ἄγε μοι τόδε εἰπέ ‘but come, tell me this’ is the usual way of asking a question, and the name and titles that follow are the vocative: διοτρεφές ‘Zeus-nurtured one’, Εὐρύπυλ’, ἥρως ‘hero’. The question is double: ἤ … ἦ ‘whether … or’, with που ‘I wonder, I suppose’. σχήσουσι is the future of ἔχω, here ‘hold back’; πελώριον ‘huge’ is a word of wonder at Hector. φθίσονται is the future middle of φθίνω ‘perish’, and δαμέντες the aorist passive participle of δάμνημι ‘overpower’, with δουρί ‘by the spear’ in the dative. The Greek semicolon is the question mark.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ αὖτ’ Εὐρύπυλος βεβλημένος ἀντίον ηὔδα·
sentences.tr: ton d’ aut’ Eurypylos beblēmenos antion ēuda·
sentences.l: Him then in turn Eurypylus, struck, spoke, face to face:
sentences.i: Then the wounded Eurypylus spoke to him in turn, face to face:
sentences.n: τὸν δ’ αὖτ’ … ἀντίον ηὔδα is the reply-formula that fits the name of the speaker between its two halves: ‘him then in turn … spoke, face to face’. ηὔδα is the imperfect of αὐδάω ‘speak’, and ἀντίον ‘face to face’ is adverbial. βεβλημένος, as at 809, is ‘struck’ in the literal line and ‘wounded’ in the free line; the poet keeps the man’s state before us as he answers. The reply fills the next units.

sentences.t:
οὐκέτι διογενὲς Πατρόκλεες ἄλκαρ Ἀχαιῶν
ἔσσεται, ἀλλ’ ἐν νηυσὶ μελαίνῃσιν πεσέονται.
sentences.tr:
ouketi diogenes Patroklees alkar Achaiōn
essetai, all’ en nēusi melainēisin peseontai.
sentences.l:
“No longer, Zeus-sprung Patroclus, a defence of the Achaeans
will there be, but among the black ships they will fall.
sentences.i: “There will be no defence for the Achaeans any longer, Zeus-born Patroclus; they will fall among the black ships.
sentences.n: The answer comes at once and without softening. διογενές ‘Zeus-sprung’ and Πατρόκλεες, the vocative of Πατροκλῆς with the uncontracted ending -εες (Attic Πατρόκλεις), are the address; ἄλκαρ ‘defence’ is the subject of ἔσσεται. ἔσσεται is the epic future of εἰμί, with doubled σ (Attic ἔσται). οὐκέτι ‘no longer’ opens the sentence. πεσέονται is the uncontracted future of πίπτω ‘fall’; the subject, the Achaeans, is not repeated. νηυσὶ μελαίνῃσιν is the dative plural in -ῃσιν, ‘black ships’.

sentences.t:
οἳ μὲν γὰρ δὴ πάντες, ὅσοι πάρος ἦσαν ἄριστοι,
ἐν νηυσὶν κέαται βεβλημένοι οὐτάμενοί τε
χερσὶν ὕπο Τρώων·
sentences.tr:
hoi men gar dē pantes, hosoi paros ēsan aristoi,
en nēusin keatai beblēmenoi outamenoi te
chersin hypo Trōōn·
sentences.i: For all those who were the best before now lie among the ships, struck and wounded at the hands of the Trojans;
sentences.n: οἳ μὲν … τῶν δέ sets the Achaean chiefs against the Trojans: ‘those, on the one hand, … and of those (the Trojans), on the other’. οἳ μὲν γὰρ δὴ πάντες hangs until the verb κέαται, and ὅσοι πάρος ἦσαν ἄριστοι says which ones: ‘all who before were the best’. κέαται is the epic third plural of κεῖμαι (Attic κεῖνται), ‘lie’. βεβλημένοι οὐτάμενοί τε are two different words for being hit, βάλλω ‘strike’ and οὐτάω ‘wound’, and the English keeps them apart. χερσὶν ὕπο Τρώων is ‘under the hands of the Trojans’, with ὕπο after its noun, which is why the accent falls on the first syllable.

sentences.t: τῶν δὲ σθένος ὄρνυται αἰέν.
sentences.tr: tōn de sthenos ornytai aien.
sentences.l: but of them the strength rises always.
sentences.i: but their strength is always rising.
sentences.n: τῶν δέ ‘but of those’ answers οἳ μέν two lines before, in the last unit: the Trojans, in contrast to the fallen chiefs. σθένος is ‘strength’. ὄρνυται is the present middle of ὄρνυμι, ‘rouse, rise’, and αἰέν is the epic form of ἀεί ‘always’. The sentence is the reason why the Achaeans will fall.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ ἐμὲ μὲν σὺ σάωσον ἄγων ἐπὶ νῆα μέλαιναν,
sentences.tr: all’ eme men sy saōson agōn epi nēa melainan,
sentences.l: But me, you, save, leading me to a black ship,
sentences.i: But you, save me, and take me to a black ship,
sentences.n: ἐμὲ μὲν σύ puts ‘me’ and ‘you’ side by side, both stressed, and the request begins: ‘me, you save’. σάωσον is the aorist imperative of σαόω ‘save’ (Attic σῶσον), and ἄγων ‘leading, taking’ shows how: by taking him to a ship. The Greek says only ἐπὶ νῆα μέλαιναν ‘to a black ship’, singular. The orders that follow are all in the imperative.

sentences.t:
μηροῦ δ’ ἔκταμ’ ὀϊστόν, ἀπ’ αὐτοῦ δ’ αἷμα κελαινὸν
νίζ’ ὕδατι λιαρῷ, ἐπὶ δ’ ἤπια φάρμακα πάσσε
ἐσθλά, τά σε προτί φασιν Ἀχιλλῆος δεδιδάχθαι,
ὃν Χείρων ἐδίδαξε δικαιότατος Κενταύρων.
sentences.tr:
mērou d’ ektam’ oïston, ap’ autou d’ haima kelainon
niz’ hydati liarōi, epi d’ ēpia pharmaka passe
esthla, ta se proti phasin Achillēos dedidachthai,
hon Cheirōn edidaxe dikaiotatos Kentaurōn.
sentences.l:
and from the thigh cut out the arrow, and from it the dark blood
wash with warm water, and upon it gentle drugs sprinkle,
good ones, which they say you have been taught by Achilles,
whom Chiron taught, most just of the Centaurs.
sentences.i: Cut the arrow out of my thigh, wash the dark blood from it with warm water, and sprinkle on it gentle drugs, good ones, of the kind they say you have been taught by Achilles, whom Chiron taught, the most just of the Centaurs.
sentences.n: A run of commands: ἔκταμ’ (aorist imperative of ἐκτάμνω ‘cut out’), νίζ’ (imperative of νίζω ‘wash’) and ἐπὶ … πάσσε (tmesis; ‘sprinkle on’). μηροῦ is the genitive of the thing cut out of; ἀπ’ αὐτοῦ ‘from it’ looks back most naturally to the thigh. ἤπια φάρμακα ‘gentle drugs’ are ἐσθλά ‘good’, and τά is the relative. σε προτί … Ἀχιλλῆος δεδιδάχθαι is ‘you have been taught by Achilles’: προτί is πρός, and with the genitive it says from whom; δεδιδάχθαι is the perfect passive infinitive of διδάσκω. φασιν ‘they say’ makes it hearsay. ὃν Χείρων ἐδίδαξε: ὅν is Achilles, ‘whom Chiron taught’. δικαιότατος Κενταύρων is ‘the most just of the Centaurs’.

sentences.t:
ἰητροὶ μὲν γὰρ Ποδαλείριος ἠδὲ Μαχάων
τὸν μὲν ἐνὶ κλισίῃσιν ὀΐομαι ἕλκος ἔχοντα
χρηΐζοντα καὶ αὐτὸν ἀμύμονος ἰητῆρος
κεῖσθαι·
sentences.tr:
iētroi men gar Podaleirios ēde Machaōn
ton men eni klisiēisin oïomai helkos echonta
chrēïzonta kai auton amymonos iētēros
keisthai·
sentences.l:
For the healers, Podalirius and Machaon,
the one, in the huts, I think, having a wound,
needing himself also a blameless healer,
to lie;
sentences.i: For as for the healers Podalirius and Machaon, I think the one lies in the huts with a wound, in need himself of a blameless healer;
sentences.n: ἰητροί ‘healers’ with the two names stands first, like ‘as for the healers’, and the sentence turns to τὸν μέν ‘the one’ (answered by ὁ δέ in the next unit). The one in the huts is Machaon, wounded earlier in this book. ὀΐομαι ‘I think’ governs the infinitive κεῖσθαι ‘lies’, which stands last; the participles ἔχοντα and χρηΐζοντα ‘having’ and ‘needing’ (with the genitive) go with τόν. καὶ αὐτόν is ‘himself too’: the healer needs a healer. ἀμύμονος ‘blameless’ keeps the house rendering, but the real sense of ἀμύμων is not known.

sentences.t: ὃ δ’ ἐν πεδίῳ Τρώων μένει ὀξὺν Ἄρηα.
sentences.tr: ho d’ en pediōi Trōōn menei oxyn Arēa.
sentences.l: and the other in the plain awaits the Trojans’ sharp Ares.”
sentences.i: while the other waits in the plain for the Trojans’ keen battle.”
sentences.n: ὃ δ’ ‘but the other’ answers τὸν μέν; he is the second healer, Podalirius. μένει is the present of μένω ‘wait for’, with accusative ὀξὺν Ἄρηα. Ἄρηα is the god’s name used for war itself, so ‘sharp Ares’ in the literal line is ‘keen battle’ in the free line. Τρώων ‘of the Trojans’ is the genitive with Ἄρηα. This ends Eurypylus’ speech.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ αὖτε προσέειπε Μενοιτίου ἄλκιμος υἱός·
sentences.tr: ton d’ aute proseeipe Menoitiou alkimos huios·
sentences.l: Him then in turn addressed Menoetius’ sturdy son:
sentences.i: Then Menoetius’ sturdy son spoke to him in turn:
sentences.n: τὸν δ’ αὖτε προσέειπε … is the reply-formula with αὖτε ‘in turn’, and Μενοιτίου ἄλκιμος υἱός is again the name for Patroclus, ‘Menoetius’ sturdy son’. προσέειπε is the aorist of προσεῖπον ‘speak to, address’ in its uncontracted epic spelling. The line closes with ‘·’ because the speech follows.

sentences.t: πῶς τὰρ ἔοι τάδε ἔργα;
sentences.tr: pōs tar eoi tade erga;
sentences.l: “How then might these deeds be?
sentences.i: “How then could these matters be so?
sentences.n: Patroclus’ question is about the double pull on him: the message to Achilles and the wounded man in front of him. πῶς τὰρ: the edition prints τὰρ as one word, and it does the work of τ’ ἄρ in τίς τ’ ἄρ σφωε at 1.8, a lively ‘then’ in a question. ἔοι is the optative of εἰμί (Attic εἴη), ‘might be’, and τάδε ἔργα is ‘these deeds, these matters’.

sentences.t: τί ῥέξομεν Εὐρύπυλ’ ἥρως;
sentences.tr: ti rhexomen Eurypyl’ hērōs;
sentences.l: What shall we do, Eurypylus, hero?
sentences.i: What are we to do, Eurypylus, hero?
sentences.n: τί ῥέξομεν; ‘what shall we do?’ is a deliberating question with ῥέξομεν, the future (or aorist subjunctive) of ῥέζω ‘do’; ‘we’ is the two of them. Εὐρύπυλ’ ἥρως is the same address as at 819, without διοτρεφές; ἥρως is a courteous ‘hero’ for a warrior, and the house rendering is ‘hero’.

sentences.t:
ἔρχομαι ὄφρ’ Ἀχιλῆϊ δαΐφρονι μῦθον ἐνίσπω
ὃν Νέστωρ ἐπέτελλε Γερήνιος οὖρος Ἀχαιῶν·
sentences.tr:
erchomai ophr’ Achilēï daïphroni mython enispō
hon Nestōr epetelle Gerēnios ouros Achaiōn·
sentences.l:
I am going so that to wise-minded Achilles the word I may tell
which Nestor enjoined, the Gerenian, warden of the Achaeans;
sentences.i: I am on my way so that I may tell wise-hearted Achilles the word that Nestor the Gerenian, warden of the Achaeans, gave instructions for;
sentences.n: ἔρχομαι ὄφρ’ … ἐνίσπω: ὄφρα with the aorist subjunctive ἐνίσπω (from ἐνέπω ‘tell’) gives the purpose, ‘so that I may tell’. Ἀχιλῆϊ δαΐφρονι is the dative; δαΐφρων is rendered ‘wise-minded’ in the literal line, ‘wise-hearted’ in the free line, but whether it means ‘wise’ or ‘fierce’ is disputed. μῦθον ὅν: the relative picks up ‘the word’, which Nestor ἐπέτελλε ‘enjoined, gave instructions’ in his speech in the last part. Γερήνιος is Nestor’s standing epithet, ‘the Gerenian’, and οὖρος Ἀχαιῶν ‘warden of the Achaeans’ is the one that follows it.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ οὐδ’ ὧς περ σεῖο μεθήσω τειρομένοιο.
sentences.tr: all’ oud’ hōs per seio methēsō teiromenoio.
sentences.l: but not even so will I let you go, being worn down.”
sentences.i: But even so I will not leave you, worn down as you are.”
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ οὐδ’ ὧς περ ‘but not even so’ answers the question he has just asked himself: the message is urgent, but he will stay. μεθήσω is the future of μεθίημι ‘let go, leave’, which takes the genitive σεῖο (the epic genitive of σύ, Attic σοῦ). τειρομένοιο is the present passive participle of τείρω ‘wear down’, genitive agreeing with σεῖο. His speech ends here.

sentences.t:
ἦ, καὶ ὑπὸ στέρνοιο λαβὼν ἄγε ποιμένα λαῶν
ἐς κλισίην·
sentences.tr:
ē, kai hypo sternoio labōn age poimena laōn
es klisiēn·
sentences.l:
He spoke, and taking him under the breast he led the shepherd of the people
to the hut;
sentences.i: So he said, and, taking him under the breast, he led the shepherd of the people to the hut;
sentences.n: ἦ, καί ‘he spoke, and’ closes the speech and starts the action, a formula the edition marks with a comma after ἦ. ὑπὸ στέρνοιο λαβών is ‘taking him under the breast’, that is, holding him up by the breast; στέρνοιο is the genitive in -οιο. ἄγε is the unaugmented imperfect of ἄγω ‘lead’. ποιμένα λαῶν ‘shepherd of the people’ is a title of a leader, here used of Eurypylus, and ἐς κλισίην is ‘to the hut’ (ἐς = εἰς). The edition begins a new paragraph here.

sentences.t: θεράπων δὲ ἰδὼν ὑπέχευε βοείας.
sentences.tr: therapōn de idōn hypecheue boeias.
sentences.l: and the attendant, having seen, spread oxhides underneath.
sentences.i: and the attendant saw them and spread oxhides underneath.
sentences.n: θεράπων ‘attendant’ is the man in the hut; ἰδών ‘having seen’ has no stated object, which is the two men coming in. ὑπέχευε is the aorist of ὑποχέω, ‘pour or spread under’, and βοείας ‘oxhides’ are what the wounded man will lie on.

sentences.t:
ἔνθά μιν ἐκτανύσας ἐκ μηροῦ τάμνε μαχαίρῃ
ὀξὺ βέλος περιπευκές,
sentences.tr:
entha min ektanysas ek mērou tamne machairēi
oxy belos peripeukes,
sentences.l:
There, having stretched him out, from the thigh he cut with a knife
the sharp shaft, very sharp,
sentences.i: There he stretched him out and cut the very sharp shaft out of the thigh with a knife,
sentences.n: ἔνθά μιν ἐκτανύσας: ἐκτανύσας is the aorist participle of ἐκτανύω ‘stretch out’, and μιν is the epic ‘him’ (Eurypylus). The subject throughout is Patroclus. τάμνε is the unaugmented imperfect of τάμνω (Attic τέμνω) ‘cut’, with ἐκ μηροῦ ‘out of the thigh’ and the dative μαχαίρῃ ‘with a knife’. ὀξὺ βέλος is ‘the sharp shaft’, and περιπευκές is a rare word with the same root as ἐχεπευκές ‘sharp’ at 1.51 and περι- as ‘very’; its exact sense is not certain, and the house reading is ‘very sharp’.

sentences.t:
ἀπ’ αὐτοῦ δ’ αἷμα κελαινὸν
νίζ’ ὕδατι λιαρῷ, ἐπὶ δὲ ῥίζαν βάλε πικρὴν
χερσὶ διατρίψας ὀδυνήφατον, ἥ οἱ ἁπάσας
ἔσχ’ ὀδύνας·
sentences.tr:
ap’ autou d’ haima kelainon
niz’ hydati liarōi, epi de rhizan bale pikrēn
chersi diatripsas odynēphaton, hē hoi hapasas
esch’ odynas·
sentences.l:
and from it the dark blood
he washed with warm water, and upon it a bitter root he put,
having rubbed it through with his hands, pain-slaying, which for him all
the pains checked;
sentences.i: and he washed the dark blood from it with warm water, and laid on it a bitter root, pain-killing, after rubbing it between his hands, which checked all his pains;
sentences.n: ἀπ’ αὐτοῦ δ’ αἷμα κελαινὸν νίζ’ ὕδατι λιαρῷ repeats Eurypylus’ instruction at 829–830 in the same words, but νίζ’ is now the unaugmented imperfect ‘he washed’, not the imperative ‘wash’. The treatment is also carried out in the order he gave, down to the drug. ἐπὶ δὲ … βάλε is tmesis, ‘put on’; ῥίζαν πικρήν is ‘a bitter root’; διατρίψας is the aorist participle of διατρίβω ‘rub through’. ὀδυνήφατος is ‘pain-slaying’, from ὀδύνη ‘pain’ and a root said to mean ‘kill’ (the usual explanation, not certain). ἥ οἱ ἁπάσας ἔσχ’ ὀδύνας is ‘which for him all the pains checked’, with ἔσχε the aorist of ἔχω.

sentences.t: τὸ μὲν ἕλκος ἐτέρσετο, παύσατο δ’ αἷμα.
sentences.tr: to men helkos eterseto, pausato d’ haima.
sentences.l: and the wound dried, and the blood ceased.
sentences.i: the wound dried up, and the blood stopped.
sentences.n: τὸ μὲν ἕλκος ἐτέρσετο, παύσατο δ’ αἷμα: μέν … δέ sets the two results side by side, ‘the wound dried, and the blood stopped’. ἐτέρσετο is the imperfect middle of τέρσομαι ‘become dry’, and παύσατο the aorist middle of παύω, ‘ceased’. The line sums up the cure and ends the part.
